title: The resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:35–44)
hook: sown a seed, raised a plant: perishable to imperishable
tomorrow: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying for the dead: some Christians keep praying, others entrust the dead to God. Your line was rest in peace.

"How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?" That's not a skeptic's heckle from today. Paul puts it in the mouth of "some man" in a letter to the church in Corinth. It's a fair question. If a body is buried and returns to dust, what comes back? The same knees? The same scar? A body at eighty, or at twenty? People in Corinth seem to have found it hard to picture. Paul's reply starts bluntly, "Thou fool," but he doesn't leave it there. He answers with something you could hold in your palm: a seed.

First, the seed. Paul says "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die," and "thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain." You don't plant a wheat stalk. You plant a small dry kernel, and what comes up looks nothing like it. Yet it's the same life: what goes into the ground and what rises belong to each other. Second, God is good at bodies. People, animals, birds and fish all have different flesh. The sun, the moon and the stars each have their own glory, and "one star differeth from another star in glory." The God who made that much variety, Paul is saying, can make a new kind of body too. Third, the list: "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power." Each line is a before and an after. Fourth, the surprising phrase: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." Not a ghost, and not a body made of fog. Some readers take it to mean a body fully alive with God's Spirit, still a body, but no longer headed for the grave. The creed in the Book of Common Prayer doesn't say the soul floats on; it says "the Resurrection of the body." Christians hold a hope with the same shape as the seed: real continuity, real change.

If you have a seed handy, an apple pip or a bean, hold it in your palm; if not, picture one, small and dry, looking nothing like what it will become. Set one person you've lost beside it in your mind. If you pray, read Paul's line slowly, sown in weakness, raised in power; if not, simply hold the seed and wonder.
The resurrection body. Paul's picture of the body raised by God: sown like a seed, perishable, and raised imperishable, a spiritual body.
Your line: sown, raised. The same life, coming up as a changed body. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians confess the resurrection of the body in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, and 1 Corinthians 15 is among the readings offered for funerals.

fork.setup: you're Paul. someone in Corinth asks how the dead can possibly be raised, and with what body. how do you answer?
options: point to a seed: what you sow is not what comes up.
say only the soul lives on, so bodies don't matter.
fork.reveal: he answers with a seed. "thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain." then the list: sown in weakness, raised in power.

chat.says: If the dead are raised, do they get the exact same bodies back?
options: Paul says it's like a seed: the same life, raised in a changed, imperishable body.
Paul says the dead come back as new people, with no link to who they were.
Paul calls the question foolish, so he never says anything about the body at all.
chat.meaning: Paul answers with a seed: what's sown and what rises belong together, but it's sown in weakness and raised in power, a spiritual body.

Corinth.meaning: a Greek city; Paul wrote letters to its church

spiritual body.meaning: Paul's phrase for the raised body: not a ghost

Book of Common Prayer.meaning: the Church of England's old book of services
